    <title>Sure Enough to Share? Overconfidence in GenAI Video Discernment is Associated with Sharing Intentions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-04T02:33:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05844v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05844v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is blurring the line between synthesized and recorded videos, but less is known about people's awareness of their discernment abilities and the consequences of miscalibration. This study examines three forms of overconfidence in GenAI video discernment (i.e., overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision) and their associations with source judgments and sharing intentions in an online study (N = 973). Participants evaluated videos depicting everyday scenes and achieved 62.5% accuracy. Three forms of overconfidence showed distinct patterns: participants overplaced themselves by 12.8 percentile points, but overprecision showed consistent positive associations with sharing intentions and the tendency to classify videos as human-made. Age, GenAI usage, and AI literacy showed consistent positive associations with all three forms of overconfidence. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing the three forms of overconfidence to better understand GenAI engagement and incorporating metacognition into interventions to support informed media consumption.</summary>

    <title>OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T23:27:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05741v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05741v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Motor responses evoked by noxious stimulation are used to assess neurological function in hospitalized patients with disorders of consciousness. In standard bedside assessments, these stimuli are applied manually, resulting in substantial variation in force, duration, frequency, and location. Here, we present OUCH (Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic stimulation), a wrist-worn device that uses pneumatic actuation to deliver noxious mechanical stimuli. OUCH combines stacked pneumatic pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer designed to buckle at a set load, so that the indenter contacts the skin only during actuation. We characterize the device using blocked force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and a deformable pressure testbed, and benchmark it against a commercially available handheld pressure algometer. At 200 kPa pouch inflation pressure, our indenter concentrated its load into an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa, over 25 times that of the algometer tip, while requiring less total force. On the deformable testbed, it localized deformation near the surface, while deformation at depth remained comparable to the algometer. As a result, in preliminary perceptual testing, our indenter elicited discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than the algometer, demonstrating the feasibility of evoking discomfort with a compact, wearable soft actuator. These results show that combining pneumatic actuation with designed contact geometry enables controlled, repeatable noxious stimulation at the wrist, providing a foundation for objective neurological assessment.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00380v1</id>
    <title>Where Intention Goes, Responsibility Flows: Grounding AI Accountability in the Machine Learning Paradigm</title>
    <updated>2026-10-30T21:01:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00380v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.00380v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An opening salvo of lawsuits in U.S. courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and post-deployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor's responsibility by their intent's specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology's pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21506v1</id>
    <title>Generic splitting types and Terao's conjecture for seventeen and eighteen lines</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T18:04:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21506v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21506v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that the generic splitting type of the logarithmic bundle of an arrangement of at most eighteen lines in the complex projective plane is determined by the intersection lattice. In particular, Terao's freeness conjecture holds for seventeen and eighteen lines. For any number of lines, it holds for free arrangements whose smaller exponent is at most eight. By the theorem for at most sixteen lines, the problem reduces to a uniformity condition for lattices of seventeen lines: if all realizations have minimal Jacobian-syzygy degree at least seven, then all or none have degree seven. The proof has two parts. First, a realization of minimal degree seven has defect at most four, the defect being the length of the zero scheme of a minimal section. This uses the residual inflection quartic of the associated degree-seven foliation, local inflection identities, and fixed-point theory for critically fixed rational maps of degree seven with exact finite certificates. Second, the uniformity condition holds at these defects. For multiplicities at most six, a critical realization contains a twelve-line core of minimal weight, and an exact search through extensions of the cores shows that the lattice has a single Galois orbit of realizations; the only family left at defect four has no critical member. For a point of multiplicity seven we use the zero scheme of the pencil derivation and a classification of transversal structures. Terao's conjecture for seventeen and eighteen lines needs only defects one, two and three and, for seventeen lines, this classification at multiplicity seven. The proof is computer-assisted.</summary>

    <title>Polynomial bounds for quasiplanar graphs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T17:05:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21416v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21416v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A graph $G$ is $k$-quasiplanar if it can be drawn in the plane without $k$ pairwise crossing edges. It was a longstanding conjecture that $n$-vertex $k$-quasiplanar graphs have $O_k(n)$ edges. This was recently resolved by Sadhu and, independently, by Pach, Tardos, and Zeng, based on a theorem in topology proven by Beeker and Lazarovich. These papers showed that $k$-quasiplanar graphs have at most $k^{O(k)}n$ edges.
  In this note, we greatly improve the dependence on $k$ and show that every $k$-quasiplanar $n$-vertex graph has at most $O(k^2n)$ edges. The proof is based on a geometric charging scheme and Erdős-Szekeres type combinatorial arguments.</summary>

    <summary>We show that the Picard rank of $d$-dimensional Gorenstein toric Fano varieties is at most $2d$. This generalizes Batyrev's conjecture of Picard ranks for smooth toric Fano varieties, which was proved by Casagrande for all $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial Gorenstein toric Fano varieties. The convex-geometric proof is a generalization of Casagrande's proof and Eikelberg's theory of non-$\mathbb{Q}$-factorial toric Picard groups, with key ideas from work of Debarre, Øbro, Fujita and the first author. The proof was found using ChatGPT 6.1.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20974v1</id>
    <title>Projective planes with abelian collineation groups of type (F) are Desarguesian</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T12:10:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20974v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20974v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We use prime ideal factorization and residue class fields of cyclotomic integer rings to prove that every abelian direct product difference set is classical. This implies that every projective plane of order $n$ with an abelian collineation group of order $n(n-1)$ is Desarguesian, proving a conjecture of Jungnickel and de Resmini. As a consequence, we obtain the classification of circular Costas maps and of Costas polynomials conjectured by Muratovic-Ribic, Pott, Thomson and Wang and by Torres and Rubio.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20820v1</id>
    <title>Collapsibility of Vietoris--Rips complexes of hypercube graphs in codimension two</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T10:04:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20820v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20820v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Shukla conjectured that the collapsibility number of the Vietoris-Rips complex $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ of the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph at scale $r$ equals $2^r$ for all $n\ge r+1$. We prove the conjecture for $n=r+2$ and every $r$, which gives the first known cases with $r\ge 4$ beyond the cross-polytope case $n=r+1$. Writing $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ as the independence complex of the graph $H_{n,r}$ that joins two points when their Hamming distance exceeds $r$, we construct a cover of $H_{r+2,r}$ by $2^r$ co-chordal subgraphs. The key general tool is the inequality that, for every graph $G$, the $θ$-number of Bıyıkoğlu and Civan of the independence complex of $G$, and hence the collapsibility number of that complex, is at most the co-chordal cover number of $G$; this strengthens Woodroofe's regularity bound. We also show, using a theorem of Alon, Jin, and Sudakov, that the induced matching number of $H_{n,r}$ equals $2^r$ for every $n>r$, and that $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ is vertex decomposable if and only if $r=1$ or $n=r+1$. As consequences, we determine the top degree of nonvanishing homology and the coconnectivity of $\mathrm{VR}(I_{r+2};r)$, and we prove split injectivity in top-degree integral homology. Finally, assuming a recent skew Hamming set-pair theorem of Gao and Zhao, we prove that the collapsibility number of $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ is at most $2^{r+1}-4$ for all $n>r\ge 2$.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20784v1</id>
    <title>On homogeneous hypertournaments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:32:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20784v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20784v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Sullivan recently constructed continuum many countable homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for every $n\ge3$ by forbidding configurations he calls pair-cancelling. We show that, for every family $\mathcal F$ of pair-cancelling $n$-hypertournaments, the class of all linearly ordered finite $\mathcal F$-free $n$-hypertournaments is Ramsey and has the ordering property. In particular, freely ordered $\mathbf{H}_4$-free $3$-hypertournaments are Ramsey, answering a question of Cherlin, Hubička, Nešetřil, and the author from 2021. For every odd $n\ge3$, we give a simple Ramsey expansion with the expansion property for even $n$-hypertournaments by naming an $(n-1)$-hypertournament and a free linear order.
  We also show that, for $n\ge6$, no unbounded hereditary strong amalgamation class of finite $n$-hypertournaments has EPPA. Moreover, we prove the failure of EPPA for all Sullivan's classes with $n\ge4$, and for the even $5$-hypertournaments.
  We conjecture that even hypertournaments and classes omitting a family of pair-cancelling hypertournaments, together with the homogeneous cyclic order in arity three, are the only countably infinite homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for $n\ge3$. We give some supporting evidence.</summary>

    <title>$L$-systems on the large Witt design</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T05:31:53Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20554v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $L=\{0,1,2,3,4,8\}$, associated with the large Witt design $S(5,8,24)$, and let $m(n,24,L)$ be the maximum size of a family of $24$-element subsets of an $n$-element set whose distinct members have intersection sizes in $L$. We prove that there are positive constants $c,C,n_0$ such that, for every $n\geq n_0$, \[ cn^{316/63}\leq m(n,24,L)\leq Cn^{169/29}. \] We also obtain similar results for the systems associated with $S(4,7,23)$, $S(3,6,22)$, and $S(3,4,14)$. The upper bounds follow from a non-Shannon information inequality and disprove conjectures of Kupavskii and Terekhov. The lower bounds follow from an algebraic construction for arbitrary Steiner systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20504v1</id>
    <title>A proof of a conjecture on bipartite correspondence packing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T04:15:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20504v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20504v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A correspondence cover assigns a set of possible colors to each vertex of a graph. For each edge, a matching between the two endpoint color sets specifies the forbidden color pairs. A correspondence coloring selects one color at each vertex so that no forbidden pair is selected. A full correspondence packing is a collection of such colorings that uses every color at each vertex exactly once.
  We prove a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, Davies, and Kang [Random Structures & Algorithms 64 (2024), 62--93]. For every sufficiently large $D$, there is a positive integer $k(D)=(1+o(1))D/\log D$ such that every correspondence cover of any finite bipartite graph has a full correspondence packing if each color has at most $D$ forbidden partners and each vertex has $k(D)$ colors. More precisely, we prove this conclusion with \[
  k(D)=\left\lceil\frac{D}{\log D-2\log\log D-6}\right\rceil \] for every integer $D\ge\lceil e^{20}\rceil$.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21597v1</id>
    <title>Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T18:58:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21597v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21597v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21251v1</id>
    <title>The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T15:28:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21251v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21251v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $κ$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{κ/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\llκ\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="cs.CL" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19783v1</id>
    <title>Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T04:18:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19783v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19783v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19575v1</id>
    <title>Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T19:09:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19575v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19575v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="cs.AI" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19566v1</id>
    <title>Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T18:57:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19566v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19566v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17603v1</id>
    <title>Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T23:53:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17603v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17603v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $Ω(KCH^3/(ε\max\{ε,β\}))$ samples on some instances when $ε$ is small, where $β$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $β\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/β$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/ε$, with no coverage assumption. For $β\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/ε$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17596v1</id>
    <title>Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T23:33:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17596v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17596v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($δ$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $δ$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $α> 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(α) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $α$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(α^*)$.</summary>
    <category term="cs.CR" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13337v1</id>
    <title>VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T23:03:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13337v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13337v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21592v1</id>
    <title>Connectivity from activity in spiking neural networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T18:56:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21592v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21592v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We show that a wide range of recurrent neural network models obey a simple set of equations tying synaptic connectivity and single-cell response properties to neural correlations. Our modeling framework considers networks in a stationary, asynchronous state and contains a broad class of synaptic filters, spiking nonlinearities, and random-plus-structured connectivity. The resulting equations naturally decompose into contributions from monosynaptic, disynaptic, and higher order paths through the network. We leverage this decomposition to express the effective monosynaptic connection between two neurons in terms of experimentally measurable statistics of the activity, and in particular, their high-frequency correlations. In this way, we show that it is possible to recover network connectivity from neural activity.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21113v1</id>
    <title>Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T13:58:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21113v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21113v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20450v1</id>
    <title>Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T03:19:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20450v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20450v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The asymptotic phase is the central object of phase reduction theory for limit-cycle oscillators. It is a scalar coordinate defined throughout the basin of attraction of a limit cycle that advances at a constant natural frequency along every trajectory. Computing the phase from a given mathematical model requires solving a first-order partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire basin, which is challenging due to high computation costs and complex boundary conditions. In this study, we propose a physics-informed neural network to efficiently calculate the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators. By incorporating three types of loss functions, we train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to satisfy the governing PDE for the asymptotic phase and the adjoint equation for the phase gradient. The trained network delivers the phase function accurately and, via automatic differentiation, allows the calculation of the phase gradient governing the oscillator's response to perturbations, which enables rapid entrainment closed-loop control using strong inputs. We validate the approach using three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrate that the PINN can facilitate fast and global phase-locking control.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20301v1</id>
    <title>Multi-output neural network surrogate for double-pulse femtosecond optothermal control of thin silicon films on fused silica</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T23:04:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20301v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20301v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce a multi-output feedforward neural network surrogate trained on a coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature model to map double-pulse femtosecond laser excitation (1030 nm) of crystalline silicon films on fused silica across film thicknesses (50-500 nm) and inter-pulse delays (0-10ps). Trained via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization on 2000 physical simulations, the dual-hidden-layer network ([40,30] neurons) simultaneously predicts six strongly coupled optothermal observables, peak electron temperature, peak lattice temperature, peak carrier density, minimum and maximum absorptivity and minimum refractive index achieving coefficients of determination R2 larger than 0.9998 across all targets. Evaluating a dense 200 by 200 design grid in milliseconds resolves pronounced thin-film interference fringes and carrier-induced index modulation, identifying an optimal optothermal coupling regime at d=156 nm and Dt=4.572 ps. This unified machine-learning workflow eliminates computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks for real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19639v1</id>
    <title>State-space symmetry in Boolean network ensembles</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T21:58:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19639v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19639v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Studies of evolving Boolean network systems have found that Boolean functions cluster into equivalence classes with a characteristic frequency distribution - a pattern governed by the Zyklenzeiger symmetry group - but the dynamical origin of this symmetry has remained unexplained. Here we show that it is a consequence of a fundamental symmetry of Boolean network dynamics itself. A Boolean network consists of nodes that update according to Boolean functions of their regulatory inputs; its global dynamics is encoded in a state-space network. We identify the dynamical symmetry group of ensembles of Boolean networks that average over random interaction topologies: for networks with $N$ nodes, it is the $N$-dimensional hyperoctahedral group, generated by node-flips and node-label permutations. These transformations are admissible for every Boolean network regardless of topology; for random-topology ensembles, including all ensembles of fixed in-degree $K<N$, they constitute the complete symmetry group. We also show that input-label permutations constitute a hidden gauge freedom of the dynamics. The Zyklenzeiger symmetry of Boolean functions follows directly from the node-flips of the hyperoctahedral group together with this gauge freedom. Boolean networks related by the hyperoctahedral group have isomorphic state-space networks and form its orbits, and Burnside's lemma gives the number of these orbits for any fixed network topology. It provides a symmetry reduction of the analysis of Boolean network dynamics and explains why the Boolean functions of evolved networks fall into Zyklenzeiger classes, and why these classes split in finite networks.</summary>

    <title>Intrinsic memory limits resonant control of complex cardiac spiral waves</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T21:57:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18969v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18969v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Resonant forcing is known to induce controlled drift of phase-locked spiral waves in excitable media. Here, we show that intrinsic memory fundamentally alters this paradigm in complex meandering spirals typical of cardiac tissue, where phase-dependent responses to successive perturbations over the meander cycle interfere destructively to produce metastable quasi-stationarity or constructively to induce stable confinement. These dynamical insights motivate an improved low-energy multi-pulse feedback protocol that robustly drives spiral waves to termination through sustained directed drift.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18840v1</id>
    <title>Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the $S=1/2$ Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T19:00:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18840v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18840v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Whether the spin-$1/2$ kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts a gapped $\mathbb{Z}_2$ or a gapless $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid remains a central open question in frustrated magnetism. Here, we address this question by directly computing the triplet gap with a neural-network quantum state that does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure. Applying a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based ansatz to clusters of up to $768$ sites, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies on two-dimensional lattices with periodic boundary conditions and estimate an energy per site of $-0.43873(12)$ in the thermodynamic limit. Finite-size scaling of the magnetic order parameter and triplet excitation gap shows that both extrapolate to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Together, these results provide independent and direct evidence of a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with the $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid. More broadly, they demonstrate that neural-network quantum states can resolve ground-state properties of frustrated quantum magnets that remain challenging for conventional numerical methods.</summary>

    <title>Regularized Neural Quantum States for Heisenberg Magnets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:07:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18497v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18497v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce an approach to solving locally ordered quantum spin systems using neural network quantum states. First, our approach rests on choosing a spin basis constructed from the magnetic texture of a classical or quantum reference state. Second, the method improves convergence and suppresses parameter-space drift through a regularized Riemannian gradient descent adapted to the quantum state geometry of the variational state manifold. Combining these techniques enables stable ground-state calculations for two- and three-dimensional chiral spin systems with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. The resulting variational ground-state energies are competitive with those of high-fidelity density matrix renormalization group calculations and, for periodic and layered geometries, provide significantly tighter upper bounds on the ground-state energy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20387v1</id>
    <title>Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T01:27:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20387v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20387v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19871v1</id>
    <title>Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T08:20:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19871v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19871v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19634v1</id>
    <title>Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T21:33:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19634v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19634v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19329v1</id>
    <title>Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T10:51:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19329v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19329v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.</summary>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19158v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19158v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The inverse protein folding problem, designing a discrete amino acid sequence that spontaneously folds into a predefined macroscopic structure, remains a phenomenally demanding combinatorial challenge central to synthetic drug discovery. While algorithms like SA offer a baseline approach for navigating dense biomolecular energy landscapes, applying SA heuristics to large sequences is inherently frustrated by exponentially large search spaces and deep local energy minima. This study proposes a scalable sequence design architecture, Topological Spatial Chunking Simulated Annealing, based on a localized, exact-solving heuristic embedded within a global simulated-annealing wrapper. To fundamentally circumvent exponential scaling walls, we deploy a dynamic solver that segments the global molecular target into shallow, k-variable algorithmic windows. Crucially, rather than partitioning natively by sequential 1D chronology, we introduce topological spatial chunking, which dynamically groups discrete variables based on Euclidean spatial proximity to preserve critical non-local thermodynamic correlations. The spatially localized sub-problems are solved deterministically via exact enumeration, while the global traversal is securely regulated by an exterior simulated annealing governor augmented by dynamic reheating and continuous elitism caching. We comprehensively benchmarked this classical architecture on the standard HP biophysical lattice against targeted 20-merA, 25-mer, 50-mer, and 64-mer geometries. Most notably, when evaluating the computationally exhaustive 50-mer and 64-mer topologies, the framework successfully bypassed widely accepted heuristic boundaries. By leveraging deterministic exact solving to vault classical energy traps, the system algorithmically resolved a novel, ultra-dense sequence-packing configuration for the 50-mer, defining a new theoretical global optimum.</summary>

    <title>Accurate qLDPC decoding under real-time constraints</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T03:37:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19130v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19130v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires reconciling the computational demands of accurate decoding with the stringent timing constraints of real-time error correction. We present Spatiotemporal Covariance-Optimized Parallel Ensemble (SCOPE), a physics-informed framework for real-time decoding of quantum low-density parity-check codes (qLDPC). By exploiting the spatial symmetries of bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes and the temporal regularity of repeated syndrome extraction, SCOPE uncovers a spatiotemporally covariant decoding structure and organizes the circuit-level problem into a layered decoding strategy. We further compress the high-dimensional evolution of belief propagation (BP) into a low-dimensional dynamical representation, revealing distinct signatures of successful and failed decoding and enabling early detection of unpromising trajectories. Guided by these dynamical signatures, SCOPE explores multiple perturbed decoding trajectories in parallel, enabling early termination and reseeding within a fixed serial iteration budget, with message-passing parameters optimized offline by simulated annealing. Circuit-level simulations of the $[[144,12,12]]$ BB code yield a logical error rate of $p_L=4.82\times10^{-10}$ at a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$. We further realize a pipelined two-arm memory-augmented BP (Mem-BP) core at the register-transfer level. Functional simulations at a 250 MHz clock yield a 16 ns BP iteration interval per arm and a mean input-to-result latency of 173.8 ns at $p=5\times10^{-3}$.</summary>

    <title>Non-Uniform Array Configuration and Antenna Deactivation for Energy-Efficient Sensing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T01:05:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19057v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19057v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper proposes a non-uniform array design framework for energy-efficient multi-target sensing by jointly optimizing the antenna configuration and the transmit covariance matrix (TCM). To begin with, a limited number of antennas are selected from a set of antenna locations to maximize the minimum mainlobe-to-peak-sidelobe-level ratio (MMPSR) over a sensing region. Next, the antenna configuration is optimized using a simulated annealing (SA)-based search, while a TCM optimization problem is formulated using Charnes-Cooper transformation and solved as a convex semidefinite program for each fixed configuration. Subsequently, an adaptive antenna deactivation strategy is developed to determine the maximum number of antennas that can be switched off while satisfying an MMPSR requirement. Finally, simulation results demonstrate that the proposed non-uniform array design outperforms fixed uniform and non-uniform array benchmarks and requires fewer active antennas to achieve a required sensing performance, thereby supporting energy-efficient sensing.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18995v1</id>
    <title>NEMESIS2.0: LLM-Aided Netlist-Driven Performance Equation Modeling for Accelerated Analog Circuit Sizing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T22:49:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18995v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18995v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This work presents NEMESIS2.0, an open-source LLM-aided framework that automatically derives equation-based performance models for analog circuits. The resulting equations provide fast, accurate surrogates for SPICE evaluation. To validate the method, equation-based models are developed for seven circuit test cases in a commercial 65nm CMOS technology, covering 15 metrics on five operational transconductance amplifier topologies, and six metrics on two dynamic comparator topologies. When tested on 1000 unseen variants of these seven designs, each corresponding to a different set of independently sampled transistor sizes, the accuracy is found to be within 5% of SPICE. To demonstrate use cases for NEMESIS2.0, the generated models are used as performance evaluators in multiple transistor sizers based on different population-based stochastic search optimizers. For each of the seven test cases, transistor sizing is performed for 100 different sets of performance specifications, with final SPICE simulation confirming that 83.3% of the resulting designs meet all specifications after a single sizing run. The rest fail to meet the specifications due to discrepancies between the model and SPICE, and require iterative resizing under tightened specifications; all such scenarios meet specifications within five iterations. Within the transistor sizers, this equation-based performance analysis evaluates ~400 design candidates per second, versus 0.14 candidates per second for SPICE-based evaluation, achieving 196-238x sizing runtime speedup, including final SPICE verification.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20485v1</id>
    <title>PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T03:51:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20485v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20485v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19794v1</id>
    <title>Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T05:00:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19794v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19794v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19763v1</id>
    <title>Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T03:44:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19763v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19763v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. A striking implication of the original work is that a model trained on only 33% ambiguous examples can outperform full-data training on several OOD evaluations, including a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD evaluated on Adversarial SQuAD. We revisit this claim in a stricter setting: open-ended extractive question answering, where models must predict answer spans rather than classify question-sentence pairs. For each encoder family, we compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics, train on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial-only AddSent and AddOneSent rows. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. These results show that clean-source cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not carry over as a general replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19643v1</id>
    <title>SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T22:16:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19643v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19643v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.</summary>

    <title>Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T03:28:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19127v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19127v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18101v1</id>
    <title>KnowVis: Dual-View Evaluation and Diagnosis of World-Knowledge Grounding in Text-to-Image Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T12:30:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18101v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18101v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.</summary>

    <title>MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T09:10:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17931v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17931v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.</summary>

    <title>Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T16:58:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17097v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17097v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it.
  We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21599v1</id>
    <title>Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T18:58:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21599v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21599v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce Hyperlyve (Hyperplane Partitioned Lyapunov Verification and Enumeration), a framework for proving the asymptotic stability of nonlinear dynamical systems, including those with neural network controllers. Hyperlyve learns and formally certifies continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) neural Lyapunov functions within a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) loop. Hyperlyve's key innovation is a parallel algorithm that enumerates the hyperplane arrangement formed by the ReLU activations of deep networks and certifies that Lyapunov conditions hold within each polyhedral region. We derive sound and complete regional tests to verify the asymptotic stability of the exact smooth dynamics (rather than a piecewise-linear approximation) within a compact domain of interest. Furthermore, we formally characterize the computational complexity of the CPA neural Lyapunov verification problem as co-NP-complete, filling a key gap in the literature. Empirical results demonstrate that Hyperlyve enumerates ReLU networks over 150-times faster than competing tools, which contributes to Hyperlyve proving the asymptotic stability of systems that are currently intractable for state-of-the-art verifiers.</summary>

    <title>Harmonic-Mean Aggregation of Continuous-Time Markov Chains with Reachability Error Bounds</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T16:54:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21402v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21402v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Abstracting a continuous-time Markov chain by grouping its states into blocks raises a fundamental question: which rates should the abstract chain use when states within a block have different exit rates and transition probabilities? We study harmonic-mean aggregation, which matches the mean waiting time and next-block distribution of a local experiment that uniformly selects a state within the block and observes its next jump. Equivalently, the abstract transition rates are averages of the concrete rates with inverse-exit-rate weights. Since the aggregation does not preserve reachability probabilities in general, we derive theoretical error bounds for time-bounded reachability. We decompose the error into a blockwise mean and centered-within-block deviations, and show that the rate mismatch has zero weighted mean. Exploiting this cancellation and differences between abstract reachability values, we obtain bounds valid at every time horizon through a linear comparison system with two quantities per block, without computing concrete reachability values. All results are formalized and proven in Lean 4.</summary>

    <title>Connecting Extended Modal Dependence Logics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T15:55:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21287v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21287v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider three natural extensions of the basic decidable dependence logic LFD, adding, respectively, conditional dependence atoms, independence atoms, and identity atoms between variables. We show that these systems are all connected to first-order logic with identity by SAT reductions and in several cases also faithful translations. In particular, this implies that all these extended modal-style dependence logics are undecidable. This solves a number of problems left open in the original publication [1] introducing the LFD framework. The definitions and proofs presented here were found by ChatGPT and checked and streamlined as needed by the authors. At the end, we provide some discussion of what new things we learnt about dependence logics and about the methodology of using AI in logical research.</summary>

    <title>Going Deep Inside Public Announcement Logic</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T14:22:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21157v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21157v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) is a family of logics that extend Epistemic Logic by adding dynamic modalities to the language, which represent communication and yield updates of knowledge. Among its various systems, Public Announcement Logic (PAL) provides a simple and interesting framework to analyse how knowledge gets updated through public communication. While its semantics has been extensively studied, its proof-theory remains more fragmented. In particular, the structural analysis of the announcements and their composition is yet to be refined. Deep inference naturally appears as well suited proof formalism when it comes to decompose formulas from the inside. It also offers a formalism with less syntax, that dispenses with bureaucracy. This paper presents the first deep inference proof system for PAL, using the formalism of open deduction. We show soundness, completeness, and cut admissibility for the new system.</summary>
