    <title>A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T01:10:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22043v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22043v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21958v1</id>
    <title>Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T22:39:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21958v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21958v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23174v1</id>
    <title>Inference after coding agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:22:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23174v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23174v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23075v1</id>
    <title>Exploring Students' Insights on Creating Videos to Learn Software Design and Engineering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:02:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23075v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23075v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This research-to-practice study examines the use of student-created instructional videos as an active learning strategy in a large undergraduate Software Design and Engineering (SWE) course. Supporting engagement and understanding in large-scale computer science (CS) courses remains a challenge, as instruction often relies on automated activities and summative assessments that prioritize grading over meaningful learning. This can make the learning experience feel impersonal, leading to frustration, anxiety, and confusion, especially when students face complex topics or new programming tools. To address these issues, we implemented a learner-centered strategy grounded in the principle of ``learning by teaching," where students created instructional videos to explain course concepts in their own words. This approach allowed students to take ownership of their learning, adapting the material to fit their individual perspectives and reinforcing their understanding through explanation. We report on students' reflections from a large introductory SWE course (over 700 students), analyzing their open-ended feedback on the benefits and drawbacks of the strategy. Students highlighted increased engagement and learning, and many appreciated the flexibility of the video-based format compared to traditional multiple-choice exams, which they found more restrictive. However, students also noted that the video creation process was time-consuming. This study contributes to the growing conversation on active learning in computing and engineering education by showcasing the potential of student-created instructional videos to enhance student agency, motivation, and conceptual understanding in large-scale learning environments.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23067v1</id>
    <title>Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T16:56:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23067v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23067v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22956v1</id>
    <title>Is model self-assessment enough for diverse LVLM ensembles?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T15:43:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22956v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22956v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.</summary>

    <title>Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T14:21:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22841v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22841v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22605v1</id>
    <title>Simplicity Goes Far: Auditing Prompt Optimizers with Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T11:22:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22605v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22605v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Automatic prompt optimization is growing more elaborate. Recent methods stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search. These methods share a generate-and-select step; without controlling for it, reported gains may conflate the contributions of optimizer mechanisms and larger sampling budgets. We isolate this step as Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search (DCPS), repurposing the Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) recipe as a mechanism-attribution control: it freezes the generator, conditions it on randomly sampled demonstrations, scores candidates on validation data, and keeps the best---no learned update, reflection, or evolution. Across two optimizer families, DCPS replaces Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in StablePrompt, matching classification accuracy within 0.5 pp at roughly one-third the measured cost; in DSPy-based compound AI systems, under the reported budgets, it matches GEPA's macro accuracy on GPT-4.1-mini while using 55% fewer rollouts at 32% lower measured API cost on average. The audit reveals a task-dependent pattern: proposal and selection recover much of heavier optimizers' performance on structured and instruction-following tasks, while additional mechanisms retain advantages in some open-ended and reasoning-heavy settings. We recommend benchmarking prompt optimizers against generate-and-select controls and reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/bhc6/DCPS.</summary>

    <title>HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T08:18:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22362v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22362v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, full- query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points and from 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points. GPT-6-Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22318v1</id>
    <title>Breaking Visual Conventions: Spectrally Coupled Weight Perturbation for Creative Image Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T07:16:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22318v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22318v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Text-to-image (T2I) models often produce high-quality images that follow familiar visual conventions, even in response to open-ended prompts such as ``a creative [CLS]''. Existing methods encourage novelty by exploring semantic conditions or modifying features and guidance during denoising. Pretrained weights offer a complementary source of creative variation, but unstructured perturbations can have little visual effect or degrade image quality. We introduce Coupled Spectral Perturbation (CosPert), a training-free method that targets attention projections in layers identified by a one-time sensitivity analysis. For each projection, CosPert uses a shared random transformation and its transpose to couple updates to the singular-vector factors while perturbing the spectral gains. A common relative budget calibrates the magnitude of weight changes across projections, and a sigmoid schedule concentrates their influence in early denoising and gradually attenuates them during refinement. CosPert provides plug-and-play creativity enhancement at inference time. Once the perturbations are prepared, sampling requires no auxiliary networks or additional model evaluations. On both FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, CosPert enhances visual creativity, producing more varied object structures while preserving category identity. Across 50 object categories, CosPert achieves the highest mean CREward among the evaluated methods while maintaining strong prompt alignment.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23003v1</id>
    <title>Probabilistic Simple Types for Almost-Sure Termination (Extended Version)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T16:18:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23003v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23003v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present a type system for almost-sure termination (AST) in higher-order probabilistic computation. Our vehicle is the recent Functional Machine Calculus (FMC), which combines the lambda-calculus with effectful imperative computation. Importantly for our purpose, it models branching and looping computation with sum types and a typed iterator construct. Our key observation is that by replacing sum types with probability distributions, types ensure that iteration has a non-zero chance of exiting, which then gives AST in a simple and natural way.
  Concretely, our type system assigns explicit probability distributions to termination outcomes, allowing probabilistic behaviour to be tracked compositionally at the type level. Types then soundly guarantee almost-sure termination, even in the presence of higher-order functions. The fragment of ground terms, which consists purely of the branching and iteration constructs with probabilistic sampling, is equivalent to finite Markov chains and is positively AST (expected evaluation time is finite). The full calculus is more expressive, which we demonstrate through an example term with infinite expected evaluation time.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22663v1</id>
    <title>A Unifying Metatheorem on Weak-Memory Robustness</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T12:20:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22663v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22663v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Memory models specify the behaviors that concurrent programs may exhibit under compiler and hardware optimizations, which often deviate from Sequential Consistency (SC). Robustness is the property of a program P not exhibiting any weak behaviors when executing under a weak memory model MM, compared to SC. As such, the algorithmic problem of deciding whether $P$ is robust against MM has been studied extensively, and has been repeatedly shown to be in PSPACE for many memory models, such as TSO, PSO, and Release/Acquire. However, each model has required its own, dedicated proof, raising the natural question of whether robustness admits a unifying treatment across memory models.
  In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for a broad class of memory models definable in Kleene Algebra with Tests (KAT). We prove that robustness against any prefix-closed, KAT-definable memory model is in PSPACE. This metatheorem recovers nearly all prior PSPACE robustness results, and establishes PSPACE membership for several new models, including the full RC11 and the OCaml memory model. We have further formalized the correctness of our approach in Lean. On the other hand, we prove that robustness against the KAT-definable Relaxed model is undecidable, and thus prefix-closedness cannot be dropped, in general. Finally, we implement our algorithm in a prototype tool RoboKAT, and demonstrate its flexibility by checking robustness against nine memory models, several of which are not handled by prior work.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22621v1</id>
    <title>Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T11:36:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22621v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22621v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each).
  Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement.
  By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.</summary>

    <title>Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T11:29:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22613v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22613v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22523v1</id>
    <title>Path Abstraction for Markov Reward Models: An Isabelle Formalisation in a Free Monoid View</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T10:16:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22523v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22523v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The classical definition of discrete-time Markov chains maps pairs of states to transition probabilities. An alternative, proposed in the context of path abstraction in probabilistic counterexample refinement, is to view them as a transition kernel on the free monoid on the state space, mapping paths directly to path probabilities. In this paper, we first extend the free monoid view and path abstraction algorithm to cumulative rewards on Markov reward models. We then use Isabelle/HOL to formalise Markov chains and reward models in this view, exploiting the discrete finite-prefix semantics to work with Isabelle's standard HOL-Analysis library. We mechanise the path abstraction algorithm and its key correctness properties of well-definedness and monotonic absorption, establishing the preservation of reachability probabilities and expected rewards. Proving the convergence of these quantities on relevant path sets is aided by our use of the lightweight free monoid semantics in place of the standard measure-theoretic one used in established Isabelle formalisations of Markov models. We obtain a verified abstract implementation of path abstraction in Isabelle/HOL, providing a foundation for refinement to efficient executable code and integration with probabilistic model checkers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22408v1</id>
    <title>From Attack Tree to Model Checker: Binding CAPEC Patterns to Verify Robotic System Security</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T08:46:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22408v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22408v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Security-minded verification of autonomous and robotic systems presupposes an attacker, yet the path from a threat catalogue to a checkable attacker model is still traversed by hand. This research preview presents the theory and construction of a pipeline that mechanises it. Each leaf of an attack tree is mapped to a CAPEC attack pattern and written in first-order logic as a rule: the attacker's prerequisites imply the attack's effect. Casting the pattern as such a rule is what makes it operational - its variables can be bound to a specific system's parts, and its prerequisites can then be tested against that system under a chosen configuration of security controls. Binding is our means of verifying whether a system is vulnerable to a given attack: from a bound pattern we derive an attacker model, turn its effect into a temporal-logic property, and check that property against the system with and without a countermeasure, reporting the control that defeats the attack. We describe the signature, schemas, profiles for approach, and explore how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security.</summary>

    <title>ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T08:46:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22407v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22407v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâserver topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâserver pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-17T08:46:16Z</updated>

    <summary>Digital systems are embedded in a modular environment of different components with individual goals and settings, which are often installed without central oversight. In this research preview paper we present a framework for communication between components to facilitate compositional problem solving based on explanation patterns and A/G-contracts, without the need for an oracle. Our approach uses partial MaxSMT solving and quantifier elimination to compute counterfactual explanation messages. We illustrate the feasibility of the approach with a proof-of-concept chain topology example, and discuss future challenges when expanding the protocol to more complex topologies.</summary>

    <title>The Nygaard graded piece, the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex and regularity criteria</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T04:51:33Z</updated>

    <summary>For a $p$-torsionfree $p$-quasisyntomic ring, we construct a fiber sequence relating the $p$-th Nygaard graded piece of absolute prismatic cohomology to the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex. The latter is an arithmetic analogue of the cotangent complex in which the differential of $p$ need not vanish. We also clarify the relationship between the regularity criterion proved by Mao using the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex and the regularity criterion established by Bhatt and Mathew using the Nygaard graded piece. This relationship was anticipated by Bhatt and Mathew.</summary>

    <title>Klarner's sequences have density $0$</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T00:55:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22034v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22034v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that the set of non-negative integers $n$ which can be obtained from $0$ by repeated application of affine maps $x\mapsto 2x$, $x\mapsto 3x+2$ and $x\mapsto 6x+3$ has density $0$. Moreover, we reach the same conclusion for five other sequences of similar type introduced by D. Klarner. More generally, we establish a criterion excluding stationary measures with bounded density on the profinite group $\mathbb Z_P\cong\prod_{p\mid P}\mathbb Z_p$. A density-to-measure construction using invariant Banach limits and a combinatorial argument involving rational orbits and affine words yield our density-zero results. The criterion also applies to an infinite family of mixed-slope affine semigroups.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-16T17:06:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21418v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21418v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Given an ideal $\mathcal I$ on the nonnegative integers, we study the family $Σ(\mathcal I)$ of all sets for which every $\mathcal{I}$-small modification is not a nontrivial sumset $A+B$. We prove that $Σ(\mathcal I)$ is comeager whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an Erdős--Ulam ideal generated by a nonincreasing sequence of positive weights. This answers an open question for the ideal $\mathcal{Z}$ of asymptotic density zero sets in [Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. \textbf{151} (2023), 3681--3689].
  We also show that $Σ(\mathcal I)$ is either empty or a dense $G_δ$-complete set whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an $F_σ$ ideal which is invariant under finite modifications. This implies that the family of nontrivial sumsets $A+B$ is $F_σ$-complete (hence, Borel). On the other hand, we construct a meager ideal $\mathcal{I}$ for which $Σ(\mathcal I)$ is neither meager nor comeager. Finally, we prove that $Σ(\mathcal Z)$ is coanalytic and not $F_{σδ}$.</summary>

    <title>Möbius-Pseudorandomness for Algebraic Circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T14:54:41Z</updated>

    <summary>We define a notion of Möbius-pseudorandomness for integer sequences generated by multivariate polynomials computed by small and simple algebraic circuits. This mirrors a related definition of Kalai that concerns boolean functions computed by small boolean circuits.
  We then prove Möbius-pseudorandomness results for polynomials computed by algebraic circuits with few multiplication gates (of any depth), for polynomials with small-dimensional partial derivative space, and for the determinant and permanent. We conjecture that these results hold in general for polynomial-size algebraic circuits.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21142v1</id>
    <title>Cassini ovals, translated polynomials, and the arithmetic of their discriminants and resultants</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T14:14:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21142v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21142v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For a polynomial $f$, $a>0$ and $b,ω\in\mathbb{C}$, consider the translate $J^{(a,b,ω)}f(z)=f(z/a)-ωf(b/a)$. We show that for $f(x)=(x^{2}-1)^{n}$ and $ω=\pm1$ every zero of $J^{(a,b,ω)}f$ lies on the Cassini oval $|z^{2}-a^{2}|=|b^{2}-a^{2}|$. We call these translates \emph{Cassini polynomials} and give their zeros explicitly, prove that the zeros for $ω=1$ and $ω=-1$ strictly interlace on each component of the oval, and evaluate their discriminants and resultants in closed form. We then prove the reduced monic polynomials $Q_{n}=a^{2n}J^{(a,b,ω)}f/(z^{2}-b^{2})$ factor into homogenized cyclotomic polynomials, satisfying $\operatorname{Res}(Q_{m},Q_{n})=(b^{2}-a^{2})^{2(m-1)(n-1)}$ for coprime $m,n$, and have discriminants governed by a Lucas sequence. We then prove a comparison principle: if $f$ is even or odd with all zeros in $[-1,1]$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $|ω|\le1$, then every zero of $J^{(a,ib,ω)}f$ satisfies $|z^{2}-a^{2}|\le a^{2}+b^{2}$, and the symmetry hypothesis cannot be removed. As an application, every solution of $\det(A(P_{n})-λI)=F_{n+1}$, where $A(P_{n})$ is the adjacency matrix of the path on $n$ vertices and $F_{n+1}$ is a Fibonacci number, satisfies $|λ^{2}-4|\le5$. This disproves, for every $n$, a conjecture of Gullerud, Johnson and Mbirika that the real parts of these solutions are unbounded.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20650v1</id>
    <title>On Primitive Divisor Multiplicities of Lucas Sequences</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T07:06:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20650v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20650v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $(U_{n})$ be a nondegenerate Lucas sequence with coprime integer parameters. Assuming the rational $abc$ conjecture, we prove that almost every index $n$ has a primitive prime divisor of $U_{n}$ of multiplicity one. More quantitatively, the logarithmic contribution of repeated primitive prime factors tends to zero relative to the primitive part along any family with $φ(n) / n$ bounded below, and also in Cesàro mean over all indices. We derive explicit logarithmic lower bounds for Lucas non-Wieferich primes with ranks in prescribed residue classes. Both signs of the discriminant are allowed. Independently, we describe initial multiplicities at good odd primes by a unique Hensel root in the recurrence-parameter disk and by the exact contraction rate of a normalized Dickson-polynomial iteration. Applications include rank and period lifting for Fibonacci numbers and the Wall-Sun-Sun condition.</summary>
    <category term="math.NT" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20421v1</id>
    <title>Khinchin's constant along deterministic subsequences</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T02:34:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20421v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20421v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Khinchin's theorem says that, for Lebesgue almost every real number, the geometric mean of the partial quotients in its continued fraction expansion converges to a universal constant $K\approx 2.6854520010\ldots$. We show that the same constant is obtained when the partial quotients are sampled along any fixed strictly increasing deterministic sequence of indices. Thus arithmetic progressions, polynomial sequences, prime indices, and lacunary sequences all give the usual Khinchin constant. We also look at a different selection rule: instead of restricting the indices, we restrict the values of the partial quotients. In this case the answer changes. The geometric mean of the prime-valued partial quotients converges almost surely to a new constant $K_{\mathcal P}\approx {3.439477971}\ldots$.</summary>
    <category term="math.NT" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <title>Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T10:12:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19311v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19311v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18543v1</id>
    <title>Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:50:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18543v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18543v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17917v1</id>
    <title>When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T08:57:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17917v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17917v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.</summary>

    <title>DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration</title>
    <updated>2026-11-11T14:13:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15521v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.</summary>

    <title>Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-10T23:55:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14846v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.14846v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.</summary>

    <title>Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T19:45:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13161v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13161v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.</summary>

    <title>Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T15:58:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10819v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.10819v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.</summary>

    <title>Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T05:12:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12953v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12953v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).</summary>

    <title>EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:50:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23212v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23212v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.</summary>

    <title>Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T16:59:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23072v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23072v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.</summary>

    <title>Safely Mitigating Grid Imbalance: A Hybrid Distributional Wide-Margin Recourse Approach</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T05:03:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22220v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22220v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper proposes the Multi-Agent Distributional Wide-Margin Policy Gradient (MADWMPG) framework: a dual-policy hybrid imitation and safe reinforcement learning (IL-SRL) method designed for safely mitigating grid imbalance in multiphase active distribution networks with distributed soft open points (SOPs). The framework comprises a wide-margin constraint barrier recourse (WCBR) module that seeks the maximal separation of constraint-compliant and unsafe actions and learns to proactively suppress exploratory violations. The framework addresses operational volatility using a novel adaptation of noncrossing quantile regression (NQR) distributional critics that track the complete distribution of policy returns. The set of behavior and recourse policies integrates an instantaneous physics-based and differentiable action projection mechanism that generates SOP constraint-compliant actions without relying on active learning. Policy safety is made responsive using an enhancement of conventional experience replay, and the safety performance of the framework is supported by probabilistic bounds derived in the paper. The proposed framework was trained and tested on a modified multiphase IEEE 123-bus test feeder. Results demonstrate its superiority to conventional reinforcement learning and SRL methods and show that it is highly competitive against the nonlinear AC optimal power flow.</summary>

    <title>Learning What the True Labels Would Teach: Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T11:48:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20937v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20937v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.</summary>

    <title>Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay for Continual Cardiac Ultrasound Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T03:38:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19756v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19756v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Conventional experience replay typically applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, overlooking variations in how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures change during sequential training. To address this limitation, we propose Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), an exemplar-adaptive supervision mechanism that regulates anatomical preservation according to source-referenced knowledge drift. DCSRL operates within a reliability-guided replay framework that selects informative historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics while adaptively regulating replay during training. For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and subsequently measures changes in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted anatomical structures. These complementary drift measurements are aggregated and normalized to generate bounded, exemplar-specific coefficients that dynamically adjust boundary and structural replay losses without modifying the underlying memory-selection policy. We evaluate DCSRL under sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, comparing its performance with regularization-, distillation-, and replay-based continual-learning approaches. Experimental findings indicate that DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, particularly under heterogeneous imaging conditions, although trade-offs remain in knowledge transfer across tasks. These findings suggest that source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning offers a promising direction for adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.</summary>

    <title>When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:04:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18491v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18491v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.</summary>

    <title>f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T16:16:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18370v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18370v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.</summary>

    <title>G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T06:53:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17814v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17814v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.</summary>

    <title>Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T13:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.</summary>

    <title>When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.</summary>

    <title>Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T04:33:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08971v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.</summary>

    <title>s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T19:07:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08615v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08615v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.</summary>
